title: Loveliest of trees, the cherry now
sourceTitle: A Shropshire Lad · 1914 · II · p. 2 / PDF p. 18
contextSourceTitle: Poetry Foundation · Housman and the cherry lyric
context: The 1914 Riccardi printing gives this complete lyric as number II without a title; the opening line is used here. Poetry Foundation describes the individual cherry lyric as famous, not as a global ranking. Typeface, indentation and punctuation typography are normalized. England is an associated place, not a claim about where the poem was written.
text:
Loveliest of trees, the cherry now
Is hung with bloom along the bough,
And stands about the woodland ride
Wearing white for Eastertide.

Now, of my threescore years and ten,
Twenty will not come again,
And take from seventy springs a score,
It only leaves me fifty more.

And since to look at things in bloom
Fifty springs are little room,
About the woodlands I will go
To see the cherry hung with snow.

title: When I was one-and-twenty
sourceTitle: A Shropshire Lad · 1914 · XIII · p. 11 / PDF p. 27
searchAliases: When I was one and twenty
I heard a wise man say
context: The 1914 printing gives this untitled number XIII in two eight-line stanzas; the opening line is used as its title. Some secondary accounts describe three stanzas. Britannica names the individual poem among the collection's familiar works. Typeface, indentation and punctuation typography are normalized. text:
When I was one-and-twenty
I heard a wise man say,
‘Give crowns and pounds and guineas
But not your heart away;
Give pearls away and rubies
But keep your fancy free.’
But I was one-and-twenty,
No use to talk to me.

When I was one-and-twenty
I heard him say again,
‘The heart out of the bosom
Was never given in vain;
’Tis paid with sighs a plenty
And sold for endless rue.’
And I am two-and-twenty,
And oh, ’tis true, ’tis true.

title: To an Athlete Dying Young
sourceTitle: A Shropshire Lad · 1914 · XIX · p. 14 / PDF p. 30
searchAliases: The time you won your town the race
context: The 1914 printing separately titles this seven-stanza poem. Britannica names the individual poem among the collection's familiar works. Typeface, indentation and punctuation typography are normalized. England is an associated place, not a claim about where the poem was written.
text:
The time you won your town the race
We chaired you through the market-place;
Man and boy stood cheering by,
And home we brought you shoulder-high.

To-day, the road all runners come,
Shoulder-high we bring you home,
And set you at your threshold down,
Townsman of a stiller town.

Smart lad, to slip betimes away
From fields where glory does not stay
And early though the laurel grows
It withers quicker than the rose.

Eyes the shady night has shut
Cannot see the record cut,
And silence sounds no worse than cheers
After earth has stopped the ears:

Now you will not swell the rout
Of lads that wore their honours out,
Runners whom renown outran
And the name died before the man.

So set, before its echoes fade,
The fleet foot on the sill of shade,
And hold to the low lintel up
The still-defended challenge-cup.

And round that early-laurelled head
Will flock to gaze the strengthless dead
And find unwithered on its curls
The garland briefer than a girl’s.

title: Bredon Hill
sourceTitle: A Shropshire Lad · 1914 · XXI · pp. 15–16 / PDF pp. 31–32
context: The 1914 printing titles this complete seven-stanza poem and notes separately that Bredon is pronounced 'Breedon'; the footnote is not a verse line. American Literature names the individual poem among Housman's notable works. Typeface, indentation and punctuation typography are normalized. England is an associated place, not a claim about where the poem was written.
text:
In summertime on Bredon
The bells they sound so clear;
Round both the shires they ring them
In steeples far and near,
A happy noise to hear.

Here of a Sunday morning
My love and I would lie,
And see the coloured counties,
And hear the larks so high
About us in the sky.

The bells would ring to call her
In valleys miles away:
‘Come all to church, good people;
Good people, come and pray.’
But here my love would stay.

And I would turn and answer
Among the springing thyme,
‘Oh, peal upon our wedding,
And we will hear the chime,
And come to church in time.’

But when the snows at Christmas
On Bredon top were strown,
My love rose up so early
And stole out unbeknown
And went to church alone.

They tolled the one bell only,
Groom there was none to see,
The mourners followed after,
And so to church went she,
And would not wait for me.

The bells they sound on Bredon,
And still the steeples hum.
‘Come all to church, good people,’—
Oh, noisy bells, be dumb;
I hear you, I will come.

title: On Wenlock Edge the wood’s in trouble
sourceTitle: A Shropshire Lad · 1914 · XXXI · pp. 23–24 / PDF pp. 39–40
searchAliases: His forest fleece the Wrekin heaves
context: The 1914 printing gives this complete untitled lyric as number XXXI, with its last quatrain on the next page; the opening line is used as the title. A literary analysis identifies the individual poem as one of Housman's famous lyrics. Typeface, indentation and punctuation typography are normalized. England is an associated place, not a claim about where the poem was written.
text:
On Wenlock Edge the wood’s in trouble;
His forest fleece the Wrekin heaves;
The gale, it plies the saplings double,
And thick on Severn snow the leaves.

’Twould blow like this through holt and hanger
When Uricon the city stood:
’Tis the old wind in the old anger,
But then it threshed another wood.

Then, ’twas before my time, the Roman
At yonder heaving hill would stare:
The blood that warms an English yeoman,
The thoughts that hurt him, they were there.

There, like the wind through woods in riot,
Through him the gale of life blew high;
The tree of man was never quiet:
Then ’twas the Roman, now ’tis I.

The gale, it plies the saplings double,
It blows so hard, ’twill soon be gone:
To-day the Roman and his trouble
Are ashes under Uricon.

title: Into my heart an air that kills
sourceTitle: A Shropshire Lad · 1914 · XL · p. 29 / PDF p. 45
context: The 1914 printing gives this complete untitled lyric as number XL; its opening line is used as the title. A Boydell & Brewer article identifies this individual poem with some of Housman's most loved and quoted lines. Typeface, indentation and punctuation typography are normalized. England is an associated place, not a claim about where the poem was written.
text:
Into my heart an air that kills
From yon far country blows:
What are those blue remembered hills,
What spires, what farms are those?

That is the land of lost content,
I see it shining plain,
The happy highways where I went
And cannot come again.

title: With rue my heart is laden
sourceTitle: A Shropshire Lad · 1914 · LIV · p. 42 / PDF p. 58
context: The 1914 printing gives this complete untitled two-quatrain lyric as number LIV; the opening line is used as its title. Britannica names the individual poem among the collection's familiar works. Typeface, indentation and punctuation typography are normalized. England is an associated place, not a claim about where the poem was written.
text:
With rue my heart is laden
For golden friends I had,
For many a rose-lipt maiden
And many a lightfoot lad.

By brooks too broad for leaping
The lightfoot boys are laid;
The rose-lipt girls are sleeping
In fields where roses fade.
